claims.text: The initial composite consists of tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix without specialized interface engineering.
A thin, uniform graphene coating is deposited on tungsten particles before W–Cu composite consolidation.
An unspecified carbon-based coating with high thermal conductivity and irradiation resistance could be substituted for graphene.
The coating creates an engineered graphene-mediated tungsten–copper interface.
The graphene interlayer enhances phonon coupling between tungsten and copper.
The graphene interlayer enhances electron coupling between tungsten and copper.
Enhanced interfacial coupling reduces thermal boundary resistance at the tungsten–copper interface.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance increases the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite relative to an uncoated control.
The graphene coating acts as a barrier to irradiation-induced defect formation.
Suppressing irradiation-induced defects preserves the mechanical durability of the coated composite.
The coated composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to an uncoated W–Cu composite under simulated fusion-reactor conditions.
The coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to an uncoated W–Cu composite under simulated fusion-reactor conditions.
Fusion-reactor service can involve severe heat and particle fluxes, extreme temperatures, radiation, stress, and neutron-induced damage.
The proposed benefits require the graphene coating to remain intact during composite consolidation.
The proposed benefits require the coating to be uniform and stable at high temperature and under irradiation.
Coating degradation or nonuniform deposition may eliminate the thermal and durability benefits.
The coating's benefits may not extend beyond high-flux irradiation and extreme thermal environments.
